title: ER & EER Modeling
summary: Turning a set of requirements into an entity-relationship model, then mapping that model onto real relational tables.

slides.markdown:
**Entity-Relationship (ER) modeling** is the step between "the business wants to track customers, orders, and products" and an actual schema — a diagram-first way of capturing entities, their attributes, and how they relate before you write a single `CREATE TABLE`.

Think of it as a blueprint before construction: catching a missed many-to-many relationship or an ambiguous cardinality on paper costs minutes; catching it after the schema is live and full of data costs a migration.

This topic covers the core ER vocabulary, its extension (EER) for inheritance-like relationships, and the mechanical process of turning an ER diagram into relational tables.

An **entity** is a distinct real-world thing worth tracking — a `Customer`, a `Product`, an `Order`. An **attribute** is a property of an entity — `Customer` has `name`, `email`, `signup_date`. A **relationship** connects two (or more) entities — `Customer` *places* `Order`, `Order` *contains* `Product`.

The modeling discipline is deciding what counts as an entity versus an attribute: is `Address` an attribute of `Customer` (a text field), or its own entity (with its own identity, shared across multiple customers, queryable independently)? The rule of thumb: if it needs its own attributes beyond a single value, or multiple things need to reference the same instance of it, make it an entity.

This distinction directly determines your table count and is the single most common source of early rework in a data model.

**Cardinality** states how many instances of one entity can relate to how many of another: one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many. A `Customer`-to-`Order` relationship is one-to-many: one customer places many orders, but each order belongs to exactly one customer.

**Participation constraints** state whether every instance of an entity *must* participate in the relationship (total/mandatory) or only *may* (partial/optional). Every `Order` must have a `Customer` (total participation on the Order side) — an order can't exist without one. But not every `Customer` has placed an `Order` yet (partial participation on the Customer side) — a newly signed-up customer is still a valid customer with zero orders.

Getting cardinality wrong is the single most common ER-modeling mistake and it directly determines where a foreign key lives and whether it can be `NULL`.

![Crow's-foot notation for one-to-many and many-to-many relationships](assets/crows-foot-cardinality.svg)

In crow's-foot notation, a single bar (|) means "one," a crow's-foot (three-pronged fork) means "many," and a small circle means "optional" (zero allowed). `Customer |—-<  Order` reads as one customer to many orders. `Order` to `Product` is many-to-many — every order can have multiple products, and every product can appear on multiple orders — which the diagram flags as needing a junction table (next slide covers the pitfall of skipping it).

Crow's-foot is the most common ER notation in industry tooling (dbdiagram.io, MySQL Workbench, most modern ERD tools).

assets.alt: Crow's-foot notation for one-to-many and many-to-many relationships

slides.markdown:
A **weak entity** has no candidate key of its own — it can only be uniquely identified by combining one of its own attributes with the primary key of another entity it depends on. A classic example: `OrderLineItem` might only have a `line_number` (1, 2, 3...) that's unique *within* one order but meaningless globally — line number 1 exists in every order. Its real identity is `(order_id, line_number)`.

The relationship connecting a weak entity to the entity it depends on is an **identifying relationship** — `OrderLineItem` cannot exist without an `Order` to belong to (this is always total participation on the weak entity's side). In crow's-foot notation, weak entities and identifying relationships are typically drawn with double-lined boxes/diamonds to flag the dependency.

This maps directly to a composite primary key or a foreign key that's also part of the primary key in the resulting table.

**Extended ER (EER)** adds concepts for entities that share common attributes but also have their own distinct ones — modeling something close to inheritance. **Generalization** starts from specific entities and factors out a shared supertype: `SalariedEmployee` and `HourlyEmployee` both generalize to `Employee`. **Specialization** works the other way: start with `Employee` and split it into subtypes with extra attributes each.

Two extra dimensions matter here: **disjoint vs overlapping** (can an instance belong to more than one subtype at once — e.g. can an employee be both salaried and hourly? usually disjoint) and **total vs partial** (must every `Employee` belong to some subtype, or can a plain `Employee` exist with no subtype? often partial, since new hires might be uncategorized initially).

This is where ER modeling starts resembling object-oriented class hierarchies, but the relational model has no native inheritance — the next topic (mapping to tables) shows the three ways to implement it anyway.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: mapping ER to relational tables
slides.markdown:
![Mapping an ER diagram's entities and relationship into SQL tables](assets/er-to-tables-mapping.svg)

The mapping is mechanical once you know the rules: every entity becomes a table, its attributes become columns, and a one-to-many relationship becomes a foreign key placed on the "many" side pointing at the "one" side's primary key — here, `customer_id` lives on `Order`, not the reverse, because many orders can point at one customer but not vice versa.

Many-to-many relationships need an extra junction table (covered on the pitfall slide); one-to-one relationships can merge into a single table or split into two linked by a shared unique foreign key, depending on whether the two entities' data is always accessed together.

assets.alt: Mapping an ER diagram's entities and relationship into SQL tables

slides.sectionTitle: Three ways to map EER generalization to tables
slides.markdown:
| Strategy | How it works | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Single table (with a type discriminator) | One `employees` table, all columns from every subtype, plus a `type` column | Simple queries, but many nullable columns (hourly-only fields are NULL for salaried rows) |
| Table per subtype | Separate `salaried_employees` and `hourly_employees`, no shared parent table | No wasted nulls, but querying "all employees" needs a UNION across tables |
| Class-table (parent + child tables) | `employees` (shared columns) plus `salaried_employees`/`hourly_employees` (subtype-only columns, PK = FK to employees) | Normalized, no nulls, but every subtype query needs a join back to the parent |

**How to decide:** pick single-table when subtypes share most attributes and queries mostly need "all employees together"; pick class-table when subtypes diverge significantly and you query by subtype often — it's the more "correct" normalized form but costs an extra join everywhere.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: many-to-many without a junction table
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "`Order` and `Product` are many-to-many, so I'll just add a `product_ids` array column on `Order` to list all the products in it."

**Why it's wrong:** cramming a many-to-many relationship into an array (or comma-separated string) column breaks referential integrity — the database can't enforce that every ID in that array actually exists in `Product`, can't efficiently answer "which orders contain this product" without scanning every array, and can't attach relationship-specific data (like `quantity` or `unit_price_at_purchase`) to a specific product-in-an-order.

**Correct model:** create a **junction table** (`order_items`) with a foreign key to each side (`order_id`, `product_id`) plus any attributes specific to that pairing (`quantity`). This is the relational way to represent many-to-many — it turns one hard-to-query relationship into two easy one-to-many relationships the database already knows how to enforce and index.

```sql
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id    BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
  product_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id),
  quantity    INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
  unit_price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);
```

The composite primary key `(order_id, product_id)` does double duty: it enforces "no duplicate product line within one order" and it's the natural identity of this junction row — this row *is* the fact "this order contains this product," so its identity is exactly that pair. `quantity` and `unit_price_cents` are attributes of the relationship itself, not of either `Order` or `Product` alone — a price that can't live on either side individually.

slides.sectionTitle: In production: ER modeling catches problems SQL review misses
slides.markdown:
The real value of drawing the ER diagram *before* writing SQL is that certain classes of bugs are far more visible on a diagram than in a `CREATE TABLE` script. A missing junction table shows up as a relationship line trying to connect "many" to "many" directly — visually wrong at a glance. An entity with two candidate identities (should `Employee` be identified by `employee_id` or `email`?) forces the question during modeling instead of surfacing as a production data-quality issue after both got used inconsistently across different parts of the app.

Staff-level teams often keep the ER diagram as a living artifact (in dbdiagram.io, Lucidchart, or generated from the schema) precisely because it's the fastest way to onboard someone into how ten years of tables relate, when the SQL alone would take hours of joins to reverse-engineer.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: modeling every noun as a top-level entity
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "`ShippingAddress`, `BillingAddress`, and `Address` are all mentioned in the requirements, so they should each be separate entities."

**Why it's wrong:** over-modeling nouns as entities produces schema sprawl — extra tables, extra joins, extra foreign keys — for distinctions that are really just **roles** an entity plays, not separate things. `ShippingAddress` and `BillingAddress` are usually the same underlying entity (`Address`) used in two different relationships to `Order` (`ships_to`, `bills_to`), not two different kinds of address.

**Correct model:** ask whether the "different" nouns share the same attributes and lifecycle — if `ShippingAddress` and `BillingAddress` both have `street`, `city`, `postal_code` and neither has attributes the other lacks, they're one entity (`Address`) related to `Order` twice, via two foreign keys (`ship_to_address_id`, `bill_to_address_id`) or two relationship types, not two tables.
